newsitem.title: USA: Swiss banks, victims to argue in U.S. court hearing.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks, victims to argue in U.S. court hearing.

text.p: A U.S. judge holds a hearing on Thursday on whether civil claims against Swiss banks over the hoarding of Holocaust-era assets should go ahead.

The 18,000 plaintiffs -- Holocaust victims and their heirs -- who filed class-action lawsuits against Switzerland's three biggest banks in Eastern District federal court in Brooklyn are demanding $20 billion in damages.
Pressure to dismiss the lawsuits has come from the banks, the Swiss government and the head of an independent panel established to investigate the dormant assets.

Attorneys for both sides said Thursday's hearing before U.S. Judge Edward Korman could last several hours as lawyers argue over whether the cases should be allowed to go ahead. Korman is not expected to make his ruling on the same day as the hearing.
At a hearing in May, attorneys for the banks filed motions for dismissal of the lawsuits.

"The judge might say to the defendants the motions are denied completely, he might say some of the motions are OK," said Edward Fagan, attorney for many of the plaintiffs. "I don't think there's a snowball's chance in hell that this case is getting dismissed."
Attorneys and spokesmen for the banks -- Union Bank of Switzerland SBGZ.S, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp -- declined to speculate on the outcome.
The lawsuits are the key remaining obstacle to Swiss efforts to calm the storm over the assets.

The banks took a big step last week towards appeasing their main critic, the World Jewish Congress, by breaking secrecy to publish more than 1,870 names of foreigners who opened Swiss accounts before the end of the Second World War in 1945. Most have not been heard from since then.
Paul Volcker, head of the independent committee investigating the hidden assets, wrote last week to the federal court saying he feared the lawsuits would damage the panel's work.

"Perhaps the greatest potential damage to the committee's investigative audit would be the possibility of public disclosure of the documents from Swiss banks collected by the auditors," wrote Volcker, a former chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve. "Such a possibility will most likely result in a reluctance of Swiss banks...to cooperate with the work of the committee."
The banks agreed last year to open their previously-secret records to auditors and to take other measures to account for the missing funds, estimated by their critics at several billions of dollars.
The understanding was reached between the WJC, the World Jewish Restitution Organisation and the Swiss Bankers Association.

In a letter to the court, the Swiss Ambassador to the United States, Alfred Defago, wrote: "the most effective and just means for dealing with these matters are in Switzerland, not in a United States court."
